question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Fear of closed spaces
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Claustrophobia.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Claustrophobia means an abnormal fear of closed or confined spaces, such as lifts, tunnels or small rooms. (बंद स्थानों का भय)
◦ Example: He refused to take the elevator because of his claustrophobia.

• The word is formed from the Latin claustrum (a closed space, a bolt or bar) and the Greek phobos (fear).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Photophobia (प्रकाश-भय): An abnormal fear of, or sensitivity to, light.

• Option 2: Optophobia (आँख खोलने का भय): An abnormal fear of opening one's eyes.

• Option 3: Agoraphobia (खुले स्थानों का भय): An abnormal fear of open or crowded public places, the opposite of claustrophobia.

NOTE

• Other commonly asked '-phobia' words: Acrophobia (fear of heights), Xenophobia (fear/dislike of foreigners), Hydrophobia (fear of water), Nyctophobia (fear of the dark) and Arachnophobia (fear of spiders).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Historians tell us how this country was divided into three.
option_1: We are told by historians how this country has been divided into three.
option_2: We are told by historians how this country divided into three.
option_3: We are told by historians how this country was divided into three.
option_4: We have been told by historians how this country was divided into three.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. We are told by historians how this country was divided into three.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is a complex sentence containing a main clause ("Historians tell us") and a subordinate noun clause ("how this country was divided into three"), which is itself already in the passive form.

• Rule — converting a complex sentence into passive voice: Only the main clause is converted into the passive form; the subordinate clause is left exactly as it is, retaining its own tense/voice.
◦ Active main clause: Subject + V1/V5 + Object
◦ Passive main clause: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: "Historians tell us" becomes "We are told by historians", and the subordinate clause "how this country was divided into three" is carried forward unchanged, since it is already passive and in the simple past tense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it wrongly changes the subordinate clause's tense to "has been divided" (present perfect passive) instead of keeping the original "was divided" (simple past passive).

• Option 2 is incorrect because the subordinate clause "this country divided into three" has been left in the active form, which is grammatically inconsistent with the original passive clause.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it unnecessarily changes the main clause to the present perfect passive "have been told", whereas the original main verb "tell" is in the simple present tense and must become "are told".

NOTE

• When converting sentences with reporting/subordinate clauses (after words like how, that, what, why, when), only the main clause changes voice; the embedded clause keeps its own tense and voice untouched.

question:
Select the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank.
The transistors are used as the main __________, which are built into computer chips.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. components.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "components" — the parts that together make up a machine, system, or device.
◦ Example: Resistors and capacitors are basic components of an electronic circuit.

• Spelling key: COM + PON + ENT + S. The word begins with the prefix "com-" (together) and is derived from the Latin componere (to put together); it is never spelt with a "k" or with "cu-" replacing "com-".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "cumponents" — incorrect; the first syllable "com" has been wrongly written as "cum".

• Option 3: "kamponents" — incorrect; the initial "com" has been wrongly replaced with "kam".

• Option 4: "kumponents" — incorrect; the initial "com" has been wrongly replaced with "kum".

NOTE

• The word "component" is both a noun and an adjective (e.g., "component parts").

• Other commonly confused technical spellings tested by SSC: accessory, apparatus, mechanism, circuitry and equipment.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the parts in the correct sequence to form a meaningful sentence.
(P) technology has revolutionised
(Q) and it has transformed the way
(O) every aspect of our lives
(R) we communicate and connect
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. POQR.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Part P ("technology has revolutionised") must open the sentence, since it introduces the subject "technology" and the main verb "has revolutionised"; none of the other parts can logically begin the sentence.

• Part P needs an object to complete its meaning, which is supplied by part O ("every aspect of our lives") — giving "technology has revolutionised every aspect of our lives."

• Part Q ("and it has transformed the way") then follows as a second, connected clause joined by "and", referring back to "technology" as "it"; part R ("we communicate and connect") completes part Q's clause by telling us the way in which we do something.

• Correct sequence: P – O – Q – R: "Technology has revolutionised every aspect of our lives, and it has transformed the way we communicate and connect."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (RPQO) and Option 2 (RPOQ) are incorrect because they begin with R ("we communicate and connect"), which cannot logically start the sentence as it has no subject of its own and depends on "the way" in part Q.

• Option 4 (ORQP) is incorrect because it begins with O ("every aspect of our lives"), which is a sentence fragment with no verb of its own and cannot stand as the opening part.

NOTE

• In parajumbles, always first identify the part that introduces the main subject and verb — this is almost always the starting part.

• Look for linking/referring words such as "and it", "which", "who", "this" — these parts must follow the part they refer back to, never precede it.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word in the brackets to fill in the blank.
The ______ to the venue was decorated with beautiful lights. [exit]
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. entry.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Entry" means the act or place of going into somewhere, and is the direct opposite of "exit", which means the act or place of going out. (प्रवेश)
◦ Example: The entry to the palace was guarded by two soldiers.

• Only "entry" fits both the meaning (opposite of exit) and the sense of the sentence, which describes a decorated point of access to the venue.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "house" (घर): A building for living in; unrelated in meaning to "exit" and does not fit the sentence.

• Option 2: "road" (सड़क): A route for travel; not an antonym of "exit".

• Option 4: "ceremony" (समारोह): A formal event; not an antonym of "exit" and grammatically odd in the blank ("decorated the ceremony to the venue" makes no sense).

NOTE

• Other common antonym pairs based on movement/direction often asked in SSC: entrance/exit, arrival/departure, ascend/descend and advance/retreat.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Care a hang
option_2: Putting an outfit on a hanger
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Showing no interest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Care a hang" means to not care at all about something; to be completely indifferent or unconcerned. (बिल्कुल परवाह न करना)
◦ Example: He doesn't care a hang about what people say about him.

• The word "hang" here is used informally to mean something of trifling or negligible value, so "not to care a hang" literally suggests not caring even the smallest amount.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Hanging clothes to dry" — a literal, unrelated meaning that has nothing to do with the idiom's sense of indifference.

• Option 2: "Putting an outfit on a hanger" — again a literal misreading of the word "hang"; not the idiomatic meaning.

• Option 3: "Caring too much" — this is the exact opposite of the idiom's actual meaning, which denotes a total lack of concern.

NOTE

• Similar idioms of indifference often asked in SSC: "Not to care a fig/straw/damn" (to not care at all), "To turn a blind eye" (to deliberately ignore) and "To wash one's hands off" (to refuse further involvement).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The company will launch the new product next month, and they are already promoting it through various marketing channels.
option_1: The new product will be launched by the company next month, and it is already being promoted through various marketing channels.
option_2: The new product were been launched by the company next month, and it already was promoting through various marketing channels.
option_3: The new product was launched by the company next month, and it is already promoted through various marketing channels.
option_4: The new product will have been launched by the company next month, and it was already being promoted through various marketing channels.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The new product will be launched by the company next month, and it is already being promoted through various marketing channels.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence has two coordinate clauses in different tenses: the first, "The company will launch the new product next month", is in the Simple Future Tense; the second, "they are already promoting it", is in the Present Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Simple Future Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + will/shall + V1 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + will/shall + be + V3 + by + Subject

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + is/am/are + V1+ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying both rules separately: "The company will launch the new product" → "The new product will be launched by the company"; and "they are already promoting it" → "it is already being promoted" (the agent "by them" is dropped as it is a vague/already-known pronoun, which is acceptable).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "were been launched" is not a valid passive verb form at all, and "already was promoting" wrongly uses the past tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "was launched" (simple past passive) and "is already promoted" (simple present passive) do not match the original future and continuous tenses.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it changes the tenses to "will have been launched" (future perfect passive) and "was already being promoted" (past continuous passive), neither of which matches the original sentence.

NOTE

• When a sentence has two clauses in two different tenses joined by "and", each clause must be converted into the passive using its own tense's rule — do not apply one rule to both clauses.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Mechanical
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Manual.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Manual" means operated or done by hand, rather than by a machine or automatically, which is the direct opposite of "Mechanical" (operated by a machine or done in a mechanical/automatic way). (हस्तचालित)
◦ Example: She prefers a manual typewriter to a mechanical one.

• "Mechanical" relates to machines and automation, while "manual" relates to human hands and effort — making them a standard antonym pair.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Surrogate" (स्थानापन्न): A substitute or a person/thing that acts in place of another; not related in meaning to "mechanical".

• Option 2: "Automatised" (स्वचालित): Made automatic; this is close in meaning to "mechanical", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Yielding" (नमनशील): Giving way easily, flexible or compliant; unrelated to the man-vs-machine sense of "mechanical".

NOTE

• Other frequently asked antonym pairs of this type: automatic × manual, artificial × natural, synthetic × organic.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined word.
Solomon's reputation as an accountant is taintless.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. faultless.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Taintless" means free from any blemish, corruption or fault; pure and unblemished, which is closest in meaning to "faultless" (without any faults or defects). (निष्कलंक/दोषरहित)
◦ Example: His taintless record of honesty won him the respect of the entire office.

• The word is formed from "taint" (a trace of a bad or undesirable quality) with the negative suffix "-less", so "taintless" literally means "without any taint/blemish".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "flawed" (दोषपूर्ण): Having a flaw or imperfection — this is nearly the opposite of "taintless".

• Option 3: "dubious" (संदिग्ध): Doubtful or of questionable value/honesty — the opposite sense of a reputation described as taintless.

• Option 4: "inconsistent" (असंगत): Not staying the same throughout, self-contradictory — unrelated to the meaning of "taintless".

NOTE

• Related words: tainted (adjective, meaning contaminated or corrupted) and taint (verb/noun).

• Other similar positive-reputation words often tested: impeccable, unblemished, unimpeachable and untarnished.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
My sister, Juliet, / got married / as her / was 23.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. as her.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "as her" contains an error because the objective case pronoun "her" has been wrongly used as the subject of the clause "her was 23".

• Rule — Subject pronouns vs. Object pronouns: A pronoun that acts as the subject of a clause/verb must be in the subjective case (I, we, you, he, she, it, they); the objective case (me, us, you, him, her, it, them) is used only as the object of a verb or preposition.

• Since "her" is the subject of the verb "was" in the clause "as she was 23", it must be corrected to the subjective form "she".

• Corrected sentence: "My sister, Juliet, got married as she was 23."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "was 23." is grammatically correct as it stands; the subject-verb agreement (she/was) is fine once "her" in the previous segment is corrected to "she".

• Option 3: "My sister, Juliet," is correct; it uses correct apposition with commas to identify the sister by name.

• Option 4: "got married" is correct; it is the correct simple past tense form of the verb "to get married", agreeing with the subject "my sister".

NOTE

• Common SSC error-spotting trap: pronouns after conjunctions like "as", "than", "when", "while" are often wrongly given in the objective case; always check whether the pronoun is acting as a subject or an object of the clause.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
a short section (as of a book) that leads to or explains the main part.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Foreword.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Foreword" is a short introductory section at the beginning of a book, often written by someone other than the author, that leads into or explains the main text. (प्रस्तावना/भूमिका)
◦ Example: The famous scientist wrote a foreword for his student's new book.

• The key idea is that a foreword comes before the main part of the book and prepares/introduces the reader for it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Conclusion" (निष्कर्ष): The final part of a book or piece of writing that sums up the ideas — it comes at the end, not the beginning.

• Option 3: "Postscript" (पुनश्च): An additional remark added after the main body of a letter or book, typically after the signature; again placed at the end, not the beginning.

• Option 4: "Paraphrase" (अर्थ-विस्तार/भावानुवाद): A restatement of a text or passage in different words; it does not refer to a section that introduces the main part of a book.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often confused: Preface (introductory remarks by the author, similar to foreword), Prologue (introduction to a play/literary work), Epilogue (a short concluding section) and Appendix (supplementary material at the end of a book).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Verifibility.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Verifiability" — the quality of being able to be verified or confirmed as true.
◦ Example: Scientists always stress the verifiability of experimental results.

• Spelling key: VERIFI + ABILITY. The word is formed from "verify" + "-ability"; in "Verifibility" the letter "a" in the "-ability" suffix has been wrongly omitted, giving the incorrect "-ibility" ending.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Verminous" is correctly spelt — meaning infested with vermin.

• Option 2: "Vomitus" is correctly spelt — meaning matter that has been vomited.

• Option 3: "Voluptuous" is correctly spelt — meaning curvaceous or giving sensuous pleasure.

NOTE

• Words ending in "-ability" (formed from "-able" + "-ity") are commonly misspelt by dropping the "a": reliability, availability, capability, suitability — always check that the "a" before "bility" is present.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
Mayra has the ability for mathematics.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. aptitude.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Aptitude" means a natural talent, skill, or ability to learn or do a particular thing, especially in a specific field, and it correctly and idiomatically substitutes "ability" in the phrase "ability for mathematics". (योग्यता/स्वाभाविक क्षमता)
◦ Example: Mayra has always shown a strong aptitude for mathematics.

• In English, we say someone has an "aptitude for" a subject, exactly paralleling "ability for" — making it the best fit both in meaning and in usage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "astute" (चतुर/चालाक): This is an adjective meaning shrewd or clever; it cannot grammatically replace the noun "ability" after "the".

• Option 2: "altitude" (ऊँचाई): Means height above sea level; completely unrelated in meaning to "ability".

• Option 4: "attitude" (दृष्टिकोण/रवैया): Means a settled way of thinking or feeling about something; it does not mean a natural skill or ability, so it does not fit the sense of the sentence.

NOTE

• Commonly confused word set: aptitude (natural ability), attitude (mindset/outlook), altitude (height) and astute (shrewd) — SSC frequently tests these look-alike words together.

question:
Select the word which means the same as the group of words given.
Choice between two unsatisfactory alternatives
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Dilemma.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Dilemma" is a situation in which a difficult choice has to be made between two or more unsatisfactory, equally undesirable alternatives. (दुविधा)
◦ Example: She faced a dilemma: quit her stable job or pursue her risky dream.

• The word comes from the Greek di- (two) + lemma (proposition/premise), literally meaning "a double proposition" — reflecting the idea of being caught between two choices.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Problem" (समस्या): Any matter or situation that is difficult to deal with; a general word, not specifically about a choice between two bad options.

• Option 3: "Confusion" (उलझन): A state of being bewildered or unclear about something; does not specifically mean a choice between alternatives.

• Option 4: "Difficulty" (कठिनाई): A general state of being hard to do or deal with; lacks the specific sense of "a choice between two unsatisfactory options".

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Ultimatum (a final demand/warning), Predicament (a difficult, unpleasant situation) and Impasse (a situation with no way out) — often confused with "dilemma" in SSC papers.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
The supermarket is open from 10 a.m. still 10 p.m.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. still 10 p.m.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "still 10 p.m." contains an error because "still" (meaning "up to now" or "even now") has been wrongly used instead of "till" (meaning "up to a particular time").

• Rule — "till/until" vs. "still": "Till" (or "until") is a preposition/conjunction used to indicate the time up to which something happens, and is correctly used with a pair like "from... till...". "Still" is an adverb meaning "up to this time" or "even now/nevertheless", and cannot be used to indicate a closing time.

• Corrected sentence: "The supermarket is open from 10 a.m. till 10 p.m."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "open" is correct; it is the appropriate adjective describing the state of the supermarket.

• Option 2: "from 10 a.m." is correct; "from" correctly marks the starting point of the time range.

• Option 3: "The supermarket" is correct; it is a grammatically sound subject for the sentence.

NOTE

• Commonly confused word pairs of this type frequently tested by SSC: "till/until" vs. "still", "than" vs. "then", and "loose" vs. "lose".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
To tell others secret information only for enjoyment is not a good practice.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. spill the beans.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "spill the beans" means to reveal secret or confidential information, often carelessly or unintentionally, which exactly matches the underlined phrase "tell others secret information". (भेद खोलना/राज़ उजागर करना)
◦ Example: He accidentally spilled the beans about the surprise party.

• The idiom is believed to originate from an ancient voting method using beans, where knocking over the container of beans before the count was complete would reveal the result early — hence "spilling the beans" came to mean revealing something prematurely.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "spill the words" — not an established English idiom; it does not carry the meaning of revealing secrets.

• Option 2: "spill the cat" — not a real idiom in English (the correct animal idiom about secrets is "let the cat out of the bag", which uses "let... out", not "spill").

• Option 3: "spill the onions" — not an established English idiom.

NOTE

• A closely related idiom with the same meaning is "to let the cat out of the bag" (to reveal a secret, often accidentally).

• Contrast with "to keep something under wraps" (to keep something secret) and "to be tight-lipped" (to refuse to reveal information).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the bracketed word in the following sentence to fill in the blank.
The media, these days, constructs ________(misleading) narratives on politics and celebrities to increase the viewership.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. mendacious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Mendacious" means not telling the truth; lying or deliberately misleading, which is the closest synonym to the bracketed word "misleading". (झूठा/भ्रामक)
◦ Example: The politician was criticised for his mendacious claims during the campaign.

• Since the sentence talks about the media constructing narratives that are misleading, the word filling the blank must carry a negative, deceptive sense — which only "mendacious" provides among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "sincere" (निष्कपट/ईमानदार): Means genuine and honest — the opposite of misleading.

• Option 2: "true" (सच्चा): Means factually correct — again the opposite of misleading.

• Option 3: "candid" (स्पष्टवादी): Means truthful and straightforward — also opposite in sense to "misleading".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "mendacious"/"misleading" useful for SSC: deceptive, deceitful, fallacious, untruthful and duplicitous.

• Note the trap in this question: three of the four options (sincere, true, candid) are near-synonyms of honesty, i.e., antonyms of "misleading" — only "mendacious" matches the required meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The group of travellers were wonderstruck by the __________ of the coin.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. weight.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Weight" refers to how heavy something is, and it is the only option that makes logical and grammatical sense in the sentence — travellers being amazed by the heaviness of an (old/ancient/unusually heavy) coin. (वज़न/भार)
◦ Example: The travellers were wonderstruck by the weight of the ancient gold coin.

• The other three options are words that merely sound or look similar to "weight" but do not fit the sense of the sentence at all.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "wait" (प्रतीक्षा): Means to stay in expectation of something; "wonderstruck by the wait of the coin" makes no sense.

• Option 2: "white" (सफ़ेद): A colour; "wonderstruck by the white of the coin" is meaningless in this context.

• Option 3: "wide" (चौड़ा): Means broad in extent; "wonderstruck by the wide of the coin" is grammatically incorrect, as "wide" is an adjective, not a noun that can follow "the...of".

NOTE

• This question tests vocabulary discrimination among similar-sounding words; always substitute each option back into the sentence and check both grammatical fit (part of speech) and logical meaning.

• Commonly confused similar-sounding sets tested by SSC: weight/wait, quiet/quite, effect/affect, price/prize.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Evaluate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Assess.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Assess" means to evaluate or estimate the nature, ability, or quality of something, making it a direct synonym of "Evaluate". (आकलन करना/मूल्यांकन करना)
◦ Example: The teacher will assess the students' performance at the end of the term.

• Both "evaluate" and "assess" involve carefully judging or determining the value, quality, or extent of something.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Misjudge" (गलत निर्णय करना): Means to judge someone or something wrongly or unfairly — this is nearly opposite to a careful, correct evaluation.

• Option 3: "Unity" (एकता): Means the state of being united or joined as a whole; entirely unrelated in meaning to "evaluate".

• Option 4: "Misquote" (गलत उद्धरण देना): Means to quote someone inaccurately; unrelated to the sense of judging or assessing something.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "evaluate" useful for SSC: appraise, gauge, estimate, judge and analyse.

question:
Select the option that can substitute/replace the bracketed word correctly and complete the sentence.
They could (always) stay in, or go for a walk.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. either.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence presents two alternative options — "stay in" or "go for a walk" — joined by "or", which requires the correlative conjunction pair "either... or...".

• Rule — Correlative conjunction "either...or": Used to present a choice between two alternatives, in the pattern "either + option 1 + or + option 2".

• Applying the rule: "They could either stay in, or go for a walk." — replacing "always" with "either" correctly signals that a choice is being offered between the two activities.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "had better" is incorrect because it is used to give advice ("you had better do something"), not to present a choice between two alternatives joined by "or".

• Option 2: "not only" is incorrect because it pairs with "but also" to add an additional point, not with "or" to present alternatives.

• Option 4: "neither" is incorrect because it pairs with "nor" and expresses a negative choice (rejecting both options), which contradicts the sentence's use of "or" and its overall positive, permissive sense.

NOTE

• Common correlative conjunction pairs tested by SSC: either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also, both...and, whether...or.

• Never mix these pairs (e.g., "either...nor" or "neither...or" are always incorrect).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.
As a result of Covid-19, the quick (1) ______ to digital training has exposed the hazards of student disengagement and the resulting consequences of lower student performance across (2) ______ courses.
The latest (3) ______ has altered the education of millions of people around the world. New approaches and improvements in the school system are urgently required. Considering the increasing digital divide, the strategy may exacerbate existing inequality disparities. More than 500 million students, at various levels, around the world were forced to (4) ______ their studies. These changes have caused and will continue to cause some inconvenience, but they will also foster innovation and future reforms inside this education system.
During a global Covid-19 pandemic, the 'pile-on effect' of the coronavirus can have long-term consequences for schooling, notably for the most vulnerable. The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. whose.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a relative pronoun that shows possession, connecting "Children" to "their basic, core learning" — i.e., "Children, whose basic, core learning... was weak to begin with...".

• Rule — Relative pronoun "whose": "Whose" is the possessive relative pronoun used for both persons and things to show that something belongs to the noun/person just mentioned.

• Applying the rule: the sentence means "children whose (own) basic, core learning was weak to begin with face a significant risk of regression" — the possessive sense (their learning) can only be expressed by "whose".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "which" is incorrect; it is normally used for things/animals and does not express possession, and is not typically used for persons ("Children") in this way.

• Option 3: "whom" is incorrect; it is the objective relative pronoun used for persons as the object of a verb/preposition, not to show possession.

• Option 4: "who" is incorrect; it is the subjective relative pronoun used for persons, but it does not express possession — the sentence requires "learning belonging to the children", which needs "whose".

NOTE

• Relative pronoun usage: who (subject, for persons), whom (object, for persons), whose (possessive, for persons and things), which (for things/animals), that (for persons, things and animals; cannot follow a comma/preposition).
